brief.outcome: Bring the p95 API latency of the B2B dashboard app back from about 1.8 seconds to under 500 ms within a month, which should take the 4 to 6 second page loads customers complain about down with it, with no downtime and with every production deploy approved by the tech lead.

ambition.goal_beyond: Customers stop noticing the app is slow, and the next slow release is caught by the team before customers feel it.
rungs: Find the slowest endpoints and queries and fix them

Find which release and which change caused each part of the slowdown, fix the causes in order of customer impact (including the page-level load customers feel), and prove each fix by comparing versions
Keep it true without being asked: a per-endpoint latency budget and a release-to-release comparison that flag a regression on the first deploy
ambition.judge: Datadog APM latency by endpoint and by service version, and the Postgres server's own statement statistics (pg_stat_statements) before and after, with real-user page load times from Datadog RUM or a repeatable synthetic test if one exists

brief.deliverable: Tested fixes for the causes of the slowdown, deployed one at a time with the tech lead's approval, with a before and after readout by endpoint and by release, and a latency budget proposal.

answers.question: What is the app?
answers.answer: B2B dashboard app, React front end, Node API, Postgres on AWS RDS

answers.question: What do the numbers say?
answers.answer: p95 API latency went from about 400 ms to 1.8 s over the last six weeks (Datadog, reported); six releases in that time

answers.question: What access do we have?
answers.answer: Datadog and GitHub connected read-only; deploys with GitHub Actions

answers.question: What are the deploy rules?
answers.answer: Every production deploy needs the tech lead's approval; no downtime

answers.question: What counts as fixed, by when?
answers.answer: p95 under 500 ms within a month

answers.question: Where do notes go, and who decides?
answers.answer: Notes in the repo; the tech lead decides

research.approach: Practitioners treat a slowdown across several releases as a bisection problem on real traces. They first make sure the latency figure means the same thing before and after (an overall p95 can rise just because the mix of endpoints shifted), then split latency by endpoint and by service version to see which release moved which endpoint. For each slow endpoint they open traces to see where the time goes: database, external calls or code. Database causes are found from the server's own statement statistics and query plans, run on a copy of production data because plans change with data size. Front end causes are checked separately, because a 4 to 6 second page with a 1.8 second API means the page waits on several calls or heavy scripts. Each fix is shipped alone and read by version so its effect can be attributed.

sources.title: Deployment Tracking (Datadog Docs)
sources.note: With the version tag set, the service page lists each version with request rate, error rate and latency percentiles, and a side-by-side comparison against the previous version (any two versions in the last 30 days) with an endpoint table sortable by % change. Needs more than one version in the window. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Using EXPLAIN (PostgreSQL Documentation)
sources.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query (wrap writes in a transaction and roll back); BUFFERS shows I/O; large gaps between estimated and actual rows mean stale statistics; a small test table can pick a different plan than production. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: pg_stat_statements (PostgreSQL Documentation)
sources.note: Per-statement calls, total and mean execution time and rows; needs the module preloaded and the extension created; resetting discards history; entries are capped at 5000 by default. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: CREATE INDEX, CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL Documentation)
sources.note: A concurrent build lets writes continue but takes longer and more load, cannot run in a transaction block, and a failed build leaves an INVALID index to drop and retry. Page shows no date; accessed 2026-11-03.

sources.title: Web Vitals (web.dev)
sources.note: Page last updated 2024-10-31 (first published 2020-05-04). Good thresholds at the 75th percentile: LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1; field data from real users versus lab data for catching regressions.

steps.name: Pull latency by endpoint and by service version from Datadog
steps.why: The reported 400 ms to 1.8 s is one number; per-endpoint and per-version series show where and when it moved.

steps.name: Read what each of the six releases changed
steps.why: A step at a deploy boundary points to that release's diff: queries, migrations, dependencies, config.

steps.name: Check the latency number means the same before and after
steps.why: Traffic mix, sampling and missing version tags can make an overall p95 misleading; page times need their own measure.

steps.name: Open traces of the slowest endpoints and see where time goes
steps.why: Splits each slow request into database, external call and code time so fixes target the real cost.

steps.name: Read the database's own statistics and plans on a copy
steps.why: Statement totals show the costliest queries; plans show missing indexes, row-count misses and scans, and they differ on small data.

steps.name: Check page-level load: request count, waterfall, payload and bundle
steps.why: A 4 to 6 second page with a 1.8 second API points to chained calls, large payloads or heavy scripts.

steps.name: Rank fixes by customer time saved and let the tech lead choose
steps.why: Fixes differ in payback, effort and deploy risk.

steps.name: Make each fix small, tested and measured on a copy of production data
steps.why: Plans change with data size, so a fix is proven on realistic data before it deploys.

steps.name: Deploy one fix at a time and compare versions in Datadog
steps.why: One change per deploy lets the version comparison attribute the gain and revert cleanly.

steps.name: Read the results against the reported baseline and the database's own numbers
steps.why: Two independent records of speed, plus real-user page times, show whether customers will feel it.

steps.name: Propose a per-endpoint latency budget and a release comparison check

pitfalls.text: Reading one overall p95 as proof of a regression when traffic shifted toward heavier endpoints, or missing a step because versions are not tagged.
Adding an index with a plain CREATE INDEX on a busy table, which blocks writes, or leaving an INVALID index after a failed concurrent build.
Judging a query fix on a small test table, where the planner picks a different plan than in production.
Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write statement without a rollback, which really changes data.
Resetting pg_stat_statements before saving the evidence, losing the history needed to rank queries.
Fixing the API only, when the customer-felt page time also depends on chained requests and front-end weight.

plan.name: Find which releases slowed the app and fix the causes in order

data.name: Datadog latency series
data.why: The raw material: latency, throughput and errors by endpoint and by version.

Datadog dashboard or APM export if the MCP cannot return enough points.

data.alternative: If the version tag is not set, deploy times from GitHub Actions stand in and release attribution is marked lower confidence.

data.name: Slow traces
data.why: Where the time goes inside the slowest requests.

routes.how: Datadog MCP: sample slow traces for the top endpoints, split by version.

data.name: The six releases
data.why: What changed at each deploy boundary.

routes.how: GitHub MCP: tags, merged pull requests, workflow runs and diffs between releases.

data.name: Postgres statement statistics and plans
data.why: The database's own record of the costliest queries and how they run.

routes.how: Owner or tech lead runs the supplied read-only queries (pg_stat_statements top statements, table sizes) and shares the files; EXPLAIN runs on the copy.
Datadog database monitoring or RDS metrics if they are enabled.

data.why: What customers feel: request waterfall, payload size, bundle size and Web Vitals.

GitHub MCP: build output sizes from workflow artifacts.

stages.name: Pin down the slowdown
stages.goal: Turn the owner's words into a measured problem, target, limits and the data we can reach. Writes BRIEF.md.

stages.name: Pull latency by endpoint and version
stages.goal: Pull 8 weeks of latency, throughput and error rate by endpoint and service version, slow traces for the top endpoints, and page-level load data where it exists.

checks.name: Data covers the 2 weeks before the first of the six releases and every release since, hourly or finer
Overall p95 recomputed from the data is within 15% of the reported 400 ms at the start and 1.8 s now, or the difference is explained
Each of the six releases is identifiable in the data by version tag or deploy time, or marked unidentified

stages.name: Read the six releases
stages.goal: For each release record the deploy time, merged pull requests, database migrations, dependency and config changes and the files that changed.

checks.name: Exactly the six releases in the window are covered, each with its deploy time from the Actions run
Every migration, dependency bump and config change in each release is listed or the release is marked as having none

stages.name: Check the latency number can be trusted
stages.goal: Check the figure means the same before and after: endpoint mix, sampling, version tagging, and whether the 4 to 6 second page complaint is measured anywhere. Record baselines for the guardrails.

checks.name: p95 is recomputed per endpoint and as a request-weighted overall using the old traffic mix, and the share of the rise due to mix shift is stated
Trace sampling or retention that could bias the high percentiles is recorded
The page-load complaint is tied to a measure (RUM, synthetic or capture) or marked UNMEASURED
Error rate, p50, database CPU and connection peaks are recorded with dates
Ends with CHECKED, LIMITED or UNRELIABLE and what that means for diagnosis

stages.name: Find what slowed it down
stages.goal: Test the hypotheses: place each step of the rise at a release, follow the slowest endpoints into their traces and queries, check the database's statistics and plans on a copy, and check the page-level load. Keep competing explanations.

checks.name: Every hypothesis is SUPPORTED, REFUTED or UNKNOWN with the trace, query, plan or diff behind it
The rise from 400 ms to 1.8 s is split across releases and endpoints, and the parts add to the total within 10%, or the unexplained share is stated
Every query blamed has its plan from a copy with realistic row counts, and actual versus estimated rows noted
Each main finding names a competing explanation

stages.name: Rank the fixes
stages.goal: Turn supported causes into ranked fix cards: milliseconds of p95 saved, customer pages helped, effort, deploy risk and how each will be measured.

checks.name: Every card cites the finding it rests on
Every card gives expected p95 saved on named endpoints, and the cards together are checked against the 500 ms target
Every card states deploy risk and whether it needs a database change, with the lock and rollback noted

stages.name: Tech lead chooses
stages.goal: The tech lead picks the fix cards and the deploy order. Ask for the reason when a top card is passed over.

checks.name: Chosen and passed-over cards are recorded, with the reason wherever the top card was passed over
The deploy order puts one change in each deploy, so each effect can be read

stages.name: Make the fixes
stages.goal: For each chosen card write the smallest fix as a patch, with tests, and measure it on a copy of production data before and after.

checks.name: Each patch makes one change and names the card it carries out
Each patch shows before and after latency on the copy over at least 100 requests, with p95 and the plan
Contract tests show the changed endpoints return the same responses before and after, or each difference is explained
Any index is built with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction, with a check for an INVALID index and the drop-and-retry step
A second reviewer finds no unresolved blocker in the patches

stages.name: Deploy one fix at a time
stages.goal: With the tech lead approving each deploy through the existing GitHub Actions flow, ship one fix at a time and read Datadog by version before the next.

checks.name: Each deploy has the tech lead's approval recorded before it ran
Error rate and availability during each deploy are read from Datadog and show no outage
After each deploy, the new version is compared with the previous in Datadog deployment tracking, endpoint by endpoint, before the next deploy
A deploy that raises error rate or p95 on any endpoint is reverted, with the reason noted

stages.name: Read the results honestly
stages.goal: Compare p95 by endpoint and by version against the baseline, read the database's own statistics, check page-level load, and check every guardrail.

checks.name: The after window is a full week with at least 7 weekdays of traffic comparable to the baseline week, or the difference is stated
The verdict states Datadog p95 and the pg_stat_statements mean time for the changed queries
Overall p95 is shown with the traffic mix held fixed as well as actual
Error rate, p50, database CPU and connections and response correctness are each checked against the recorded baselines
Page load is reported from real-user or repeatable capture data, or marked UNMEASURED
A missed target is reported with the numbers and the endpoints that fell short

stages.name: Keep what we learned
stages.goal: Record which release practices let the slowdown through and propose a per-endpoint latency budget and a release-to-release comparison for the tech lead.

checks.name: Each cause is tied to the release that introduced it, with the deploy time
The proposed budget gives numeric limits per top endpoint, where the check runs, and who owns it; nothing is switched on without the tech lead's yes
Each rule says whether it holds for this app, this business or the playbook

hypotheses.statement: One release caused most of the rise.
hypotheses.test: p95 by service version and by day; compare each version with the previous in deployment tracking.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A single version boundary accounts for 50% or more of the total rise in p95.
hypotheses.refute_if: The rise is spread in steps of under 20% each across several releases, or is smooth.

hypotheses.statement: The overall p95 rose because traffic shifted to heavier endpoints, not because endpoints got slower.
hypotheses.test: Per-endpoint p95 before and after, and overall p95 with the old traffic mix.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Per-endpoint p95 changed by under 10% on the top endpoints while overall p95 rose.
hypotheses.refute_if: Several top endpoints each rose by 50% or more.

hypotheses.statement: Changed endpoints now run many database queries per request.
hypotheses.test: Database queries per trace for the top endpoints, by version.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Queries per request on a top endpoint rose 3x or more between versions, or exceed 20.
hypotheses.refute_if: Query counts are flat across versions.

hypotheses.statement: Costly queries scan large tables without a useful index.
hypotheses.test: pg_stat_statements top statements by total time, plans on a copy with realistic row counts.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The top 5 statements are 50% or more of database time and at least one sequentially scans a large table while filtering out most rows.
hypotheses.refute_if: Top statements use indexes and estimated and actual rows agree.

hypotheses.statement: Slowness follows data growth or a few large customers, not a release.
hypotheses.test: Latency against table row counts and per-customer volume over the six weeks.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Latency rises smoothly with row counts or concentrates in a few customers, with no step at deploys.
hypotheses.refute_if: Steps line up with deploy times and latency is similar across customers.

hypotheses.test: RDS CPU, connections, IOPS and lock waits over the window.
hypotheses.confirm_if: CPU above 70% or connections near the limit for sustained periods since the rise began.
hypotheses.refute_if: Database load is flat and well under limits.

hypotheses.statement: A dependency upgrade or new middleware added time to every request.
hypotheses.test: Compare profiles or span breakdowns of the same endpoint between two versions.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One package or function takes 20% or more extra time per request, in every endpoint.
hypotheses.refute_if: The extra time is in one endpoint's own query or code.

hypotheses.statement: A slower outside service is adding time.
hypotheses.test: External call span time by version.
hypotheses.confirm_if: External call time explains 30% or more of the added latency.

hypotheses.statement: Pages are slow mainly because they wait on many or chained API calls and large payloads.
hypotheses.test: Request waterfall of the slowest pages: calls per page, longest chain, payload size.
hypotheses.confirm_if: More than 10 API calls per page, a chain of 3 or more dependent calls, or a payload over 1 MB.
hypotheses.refute_if: Page time is close to the longest single call plus render.

hypotheses.statement: The front-end bundle grew and slows the page.
hypotheses.test: Bundle size by release and Web Vitals at the 75th percentile.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The main bundle grew 30% or more over the six releases, or LCP p75 is above 2.5 s with the API not the main cost.
hypotheses.refute_if: Bundle size is flat and LCP is within 2.5 s.

measurement.window: A full week after the last deploy, against the week before the first deploy, and each deploy read against the previous version on the same days.
measurement.min_volume: At least 1,000 requests per top endpoint in each comparison window; below that, the endpoint's verdict is INCONCLUSIVE.
measurement.stop_rule: Revert a deploy at once if error rate rises or p95 rises on any endpoint; otherwise read the full window before a verdict.
